Variable Renewable Energy (VRE) – Capacity factor prediction¶

We propose a modeling strategy to predict monthly capacity factors for:

  • solar photovoltaic power,
  • onshore wind power,

in different France regions, based on:

  • capacity factor observations,
  • climate variables from MERRA-2.

The objective is to build a supervised model that, for each region and each month, estimates the capacity factor based on monthly aggregated climate variables.

Modeling strategy¶

I. Feature analysis and selection¶

  1. Data loading

    • Monthly capacity factors for wind and solar power by region (2014–2021).
    • Regional mask
    • MERRA-2 daily climate variables (2010–2019): surface radiation, temperature, air density, specific humidity, zonal and meridional winds.

  2. Pre-processing of climate variables

    • Aggregation by region.
    • Aggregation by month.
    • Addition of variables reflecting intra-monthly behavior (quantiles, variance, etc.)
    • Encoding of regions

  3. Temporal separation of training/testing

    • We simply propose to separate the dataset into two parts (2014-2018 for training and 2019 for testing).
    • We then normalize the training and testing sets.

  4. An initial “naive” regression

    • We first perform a simple ordinary linear regression.
    • With the same input and output variables for solar and wind power:
      • Inputs: the 9 climate variables initially provided (and for each, their mean, variance, and quantiles q25, q50, and q75) + encoded regions
      • Output: monthly capacity factor.

  5. Evaluation

    • Indicators: MAE, RMSE, R² on the test set.
    • Visualizations:
      • scatter plot observed vs. predicted on the test set,
      • time series on a selected region.

  6. Selection of relevant climate variables

    • The purpose of this initial linear regression is to gain an understanding of the variables involved in solar and wind power regression.
    • We represent the share of each input variable in the model's ability to predict the capacity factor.
    • We also represent a covariance matrix to see if variables encapsulate the same phenomena.
    • Finally, we represent the covariance of each variable relative to the capacity factor.
    • Based on this information, we perform feature engineering to retain the most useful variables.

II. Study for solar photovoltaics¶

  1. Study of an ordinary linear regression trained for solar energy

    • We retrain an ordinary linear regression but only with the solar features selected in Part I.
    • We then evaluate the model with various indicators (MAE, RMSE, R²), on both the test set and the train set
    • Visualizations:
      • scatter plot observed vs. predicted on the test set,
      • time series on a selected region.

  2. Suspicion of overfitting

    • We produce a learning curve to assess wether the model is overfitting or not

  3. A first regularisation technique : Ridge regression

    • We optimize the hyperparameter alpha of the model
    • We plot the distribution of the model coefficients to assess the usefulness of the regularisation
    • Evaluation of the model

  4. A second regularisation technique : Lasso regression

    • We optimize the hyperparameter alpha of the model
    • We plot the distribution of the model coefficients to assess the usefulness of the regularisation
    • Evaluation of the model

  5. Study of the data distribution

    • We do a randomized train/test split
    • We train an OLS regression with a such split
    • Evaluation of the model
    • We represent the data distribution with a PCA

III. Study for onshore wind power¶

  1. Training of a new supervised regression

    • We perform random forest (bagging) using the variables retained in the part I.
    • Model evaluation
    • We represent a learning curve to determine the model variance and biais

  2. Hyperparameter optimization

    • We represent the OOB error and train error as a function of the following hyperparameters:
    • This allows us to select the hyperparameters that improve predictions while avoiding overfitting.

  3. Evaluation of the optimized model

    • Indicators: MAE, RMSE, R² on the test set.
    • Visualizations:
      • scatter plot observed vs. predicted on the test set,
      • time series on a selected region.

  4. Training of another new supervised regression

    • We perform a boosting model using the variables retained in the part I.
    • Model optimization with the Optuna library

  5. Evaluation of the optimized model

    • Indicators: MAE, RMSE, R² on the test set.
    • Visualizations:
      • scatter plot observed vs. predicted on the test set,
      • time series on a selected region.

  1. Pre-processing of climate variables
In [4]:
# Spacial aggregation by region (Weighted average by the mask)
print("Spacial aggregation by region...")
ds_climate_region = ds_climate.groupby(mask).mean()
print("Aggregation completed.")

# Monthly temporal aggregation and calculation of statistics (Mean, Variance, Quantiles)

def calcul_vals_mensuelles(ds):
    resampler = ds.resample(time="1MS")
    # Mean
    ds_mean = resampler.mean()
    ds_mean = ds_mean.rename({v: f"{v}_mean" for v in ds.data_vars})
    # Variance
    ds_var = resampler.var()
    ds_var = ds_var.rename({v: f"{v}_var" for v in ds.data_vars})
    # Quantiles (Q25, Q50, Q75)
    ds_q25 = resampler.quantile(0.25).drop_vars("quantile")
    ds_q25 = ds_q25.rename({v: f"{v}_q25" for v in ds.data_vars})
    ds_q50 = resampler.quantile(0.50).drop_vars("quantile")
    ds_q50 = ds_q50.rename({v: f"{v}_q50" for v in ds.data_vars})
    ds_q75 = resampler.quantile(0.75).drop_vars("quantile")
    ds_q75 = ds_q75.rename({v: f"{v}_q75" for v in ds.data_vars})

    return xr.merge([ds_mean, ds_var, ds_q25, ds_q50, ds_q75])

print("Monthly temporal aggregation...")
ds_features = calcul_vals_mensuelles(ds_climate_region)
df_features = ds_features.to_dataframe().reset_index()
print("Aggregation completed.")

# Processing capacity factors
df_pv_long = df_pv.reset_index().melt(id_vars="time", var_name="region_name", value_name="cap_factor_pv")
df_wind_long = df_wind.reset_index().melt(id_vars="time", var_name="region_name", value_name="cap_factor_wind")

df_targets = pd.merge(df_pv_long, df_wind_long, on=["time", "region_name"], how="outer")

# Creating the final Dataset with encoding for regions
df_features['region_name'] = df_features[mask_var_name].map(region_mapping)
df_final_temp = pd.merge(df_targets, df_features, on=['time', 'region_name'])
df_final_temp = df_final_temp.drop(columns=[mask_var_name])
region_dummies = pd.get_dummies(df_final_temp['region_name'], prefix='region')
df_final = pd.concat([df_final_temp, region_dummies], axis=1)

print("\nFinal dataset created")

# Train-test split (2010-2018 for training, 2019 for testing)
train_df = df_final[df_final['time'].dt.year < 2019]
test_df = df_final[df_final['time'].dt.year == 2019]

# Definition of features and labels
labels = ['cap_factor_pv', 'cap_factor_wind']
exclude_cols = ['time', 'region_name'] + labels
features_cols = [c for c in df_final.columns if c not in exclude_cols]

# Normalization of numerical features (without "data leakage")
numerical_cols = [c for c in features_cols if not c.startswith('region_')]
mean = train_df[numerical_cols].mean()
std = train_df[numerical_cols].std()

train_df_norm = train_df.copy()
test_df_norm = test_df.copy()

train_df_norm[numerical_cols] = (train_df[numerical_cols] - mean) / std
test_df_norm[numerical_cols] = (test_df[numerical_cols] - mean) / std

# Handling infinite and missing values after normalization
train_df_norm[numerical_cols] = train_df_norm[numerical_cols].replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).fillna(0)
test_df_norm[numerical_cols] = test_df_norm[numerical_cols].replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).fillna(0)

# Separation for the solar model
train_pv = train_df_norm.dropna(subset=['cap_factor_pv'])
X_train_pv = train_pv[features_cols]
y_train_pv = train_pv['cap_factor_pv']

test_pv = test_df_norm.dropna(subset=['cap_factor_pv'])
X_test_pv = test_pv[features_cols]
y_test_pv = test_pv['cap_factor_pv']

# Separation for the wind model
train_wind = train_df_norm.dropna(subset=['cap_factor_wind'])
X_train_wind = train_wind[features_cols]
y_train_wind = train_wind['cap_factor_wind']

test_wind = test_df_norm.dropna(subset=['cap_factor_wind'])
X_test_wind = test_wind[features_cols]
y_test_wind = test_wind['cap_factor_wind']

# function to plot a scatter plot (observed vs. predicted) on the entire test set 
# and to plot predicted time series on a selected region.

def scatter_plot(y_true, y_pred, title):
    print(f"Visualization : {title}")
    # figure 1 : scatter plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6))
    plt.scatter(y_true, y_pred, alpha=0.3, s=10, c='blue')
    min_val = min(y_true.min(), y_pred.min())
    max_val = max(y_true.max(), y_pred.max())
    plt.plot([min_val, max_val], [min_val, max_val], 'r--', lw=2, label='Ideal')
    plt.xlabel("Observed Capacity Factor")
    plt.ylabel("Predicted Capacity Factor")
    plt.title(f"{title} : Observed vs Predicted (on Test set)")
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    plt.show()

def series_time_plot(y_true, y_pred, df_original, title, region_etude):
    # figure 2 : time series by region
    df_viz = df_original.copy()
    df_viz['Observed'] = y_true
    df_viz['Predicted'] = y_pred
    # Choose a region
    regions = df_viz['region_name'].unique()
    if region_etude not in regions:
        print(f"Warning: The region '{region_etude}' is not in the test set. Displaying for '{regions[0]}'.")
        target_region = regions[0]
    else:
        target_region = region_etude
        
    df_region = df_viz[df_viz['region_name'] == target_region].sort_values('time')
    plt.figure(figsize=(14, 5))
    plt.plot(df_region['time'], df_region['Observed'], label='Observed', marker='o', markersize=4)
    plt.plot(df_region['time'], df_region['Predicted'], label='Predicted', marker='x', markersize=4, linestyle='--')
    plt.title(f"{title} : Time Series (Test set) - Region {target_region}")
    plt.ylabel("Capacity Factor")
    plt.xlabel("Date")
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    plt.show()

# Representation of features importance in the model

def importance_var_model(model, all_feature_names, numerical_feature_names, title):
    coef_df = pd.DataFrame({'feature': all_feature_names, 'coef': model.coef_})
    # we only look at numerical features
    coef_df = coef_df[coef_df['feature'].isin(numerical_feature_names)]
    coef_df['abs_coef'] = coef_df['coef'].abs()
    coef_df = coef_df.sort_values('abs_coef', ascending=False)
    # Visualization
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 10))
    sns.barplot(x='coef', y='feature', data=coef_df, palette='viridis')
    plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel("Coefficient value (Importance)")
    plt.ylabel("Climate feature")
    plt.grid(True, axis='x', linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)
    plt.show()

Based on these graphs and our intuition, we choose to study the following variables

For solar power :

  • surface_downward_radiation_XX
  • surface_temperature_XX
  • surface_density_XX
  • surface_specific_humidity_XX
  • zonal_wind_q50
  • meridional_wind_q50

For wind power :

  • upper_meridional_wind_XX
  • upper_zonal_wind_XX
  • meridional_wind_XX
  • zonal_wind_XX
  • surface_temperature_XX
  • surface_density_XX
  • height_500_XX

In addition to these features, we choose to retain the region encoding (dummy encoding) done previously. We also add two features (cos and sin) encoding the month studied, which allows us to take into account the cyclical nature of the months and thus further contextualize the capacity factor estimate.

All these manipulations are performed using the following function:

In [11]:
def dataset_creation(date_max, date_lim, features_a_garder, pv_or_wind):
    df_ici = df_final.copy()

    df_ici['month'] = df_ici['time'].dt.month
    df_ici['sin_month'] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df_ici['month'] / 12)
    df_ici['cos_month'] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df_ici['month'] / 12)
    
    region_cols = [col for col in df_final.columns if col.startswith('region_')]
    calendar_features = ['sin_month', 'cos_month']
    if pv_or_wind == 'pv':
        vre = 'cap_factor_pv'
    else:
        vre = 'cap_factor_wind'

    final_cols = (['time', vre] + 
                    features_a_garder + 
                    calendar_features + 
                    region_cols)

    df_ici = df_ici[final_cols].copy()


    train_df = df_ici[df_ici['time'].dt.year < date_lim] 
    test_df = df_ici[
        (df_ici['time'].dt.year > date_lim - 1) &
        (df_ici['time'].dt.year <= date_max)
        ]

    label = [vre]
    exclude_cols = ['time', 'region_name'] + label
    features_cols = [c for c in train_df.columns if c not in exclude_cols]
    
    # X, y split
    train_df = train_df.dropna(subset=[vre])
    X_train_df = train_df[features_cols]
    y_train_df = train_df[vre]
    
    test_df = test_df.dropna(subset=[vre])
    X_test_df = test_df[features_cols]
    y_test_df = test_df[vre]

    return X_train_df, y_train_df, X_test_df, y_test_df

II. Study for solar photovoltaics¶

  1. Study of an ordinary linear regression trained for solar energy

We now only take the features selected in Part I. for solar energy in the hope of improving the performance of our ordinary linear regression (OLS).

# Vizualisation
scatter_plot(y_test_pv, y_pred_pv, "Solar")
#series_time_plot(y_test_pv, y_pred_pv, test_pv, "Solar", region_etude)

While the R² score of the test set is : 0.8619.
MAE : 0.0151
RMSE : 0.0248
Visualization : Solar
  1. Suspicion of overfitting

As the test R² is significantly lower than the train R², we suspect that the ordinary linear regression is overfitting.

To study this possible behavior more precisely, we choose to represent a learning curve of the model (with a train/validation split respecting chronological order)

In [15]:
# OLS Learning Curve

train_sizes = np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10)
train_scores = []
test_scores = []

n_train = X_train_pv.shape[0]

for frac in train_sizes:
    n = int(frac * n_train)
    X_sub = X_train_pv.iloc[:n]
    y_sub = y_train_pv.iloc[:n]
    
    model = LinearRegression()
    model.fit(X_sub, y_sub)
    
    # Score on the training subset
    y_pred_train = model.predict(X_sub)
    train_scores.append(r2_score(y_sub, y_pred_train))
    
    # Score on the full test set
    y_pred_test = model.predict(X_test_pv)
    test_scores.append(r2_score(y_test_pv, y_pred_test))

plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
plt.plot(train_sizes * n_train, train_scores, label="Training score")
plt.plot(train_sizes * n_train, test_scores, label="Test score")
plt.xlabel("Training set size")
plt.ylabel("Score R²")
plt.title("Learning curve OLS (chronological split - solar)")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

This learning curve suggests that there is no overfitting, as the model is not plateauing but continues to improve as the number of data increases, meaning that the model is not yet “too complex.”

However, this difference between the R² values suggests that our model does not generalize well for the year 2019 (test year).

Facing this question, our hypothesis is that we are studying highly correlated variables (5 different features per climate variable + related variables) and as the course shows, this correlation between features is likely to create very large coefficients that offset each other in our model. Very large coefficients can amplify the noise in the data of the test year (2019), which would explain the poor generalization to 2019 and the low R² of the testing set compared to the training set.

To test this hypothesis, we decide to reduce the size of the coefficients in the model to increase stability by performing regularization.

To do so we use a Ridge regression on our data.

  1. A first regularisation technique : Ridge regression

First, we use a cross-validation to find the optimal regularisation hyperparameter of the ridge regression on ou training set.

In [16]:
print("Ridge regression with KFold on the training data for various alpha values")

reg_class = linear_model.Ridge

ALPHA_RNG_RIDGE = np.logspace(-5, 8, 100)
complexity_rng = ALPHA_RNG_RIDGE

# Number of splits for the cross validation
n_splits_cv = 5


r2_validation = np.empty(complexity_rng.shape)
coefs = np.empty((len(complexity_rng), X_train_pv.shape[1]))

for k, complexity in enumerate(complexity_rng):
    
    reg = reg_class(alpha=complexity)

    # r2 test scores of the k-fold cross-validation
    r2_validation_arr = cross_val_score(reg, X_train_pv, y_train_pv, cv=n_splits_cv)
    
    # r2 predicted as a mean of the validation scores
    r2_validation[k] = r2_validation_arr.mean()
    
    reg.fit(X_train_pv, y_train_pv)
    coefs[k] = reg.coef_

# Keep the best hyperparmeter value and predict the model coefficients.
i_best = np.argmax(r2_validation)
complexity_best_ridge = complexity_rng[i_best]
r2_best = r2_validation[i_best]
coefs_best = coefs[i_best]
    
# Validation curve
complexity_label = r'$\alpha$'
plt.figure()
plt.plot(complexity_rng, r2_validation)
plt.hlines(0., *complexity_rng[[0, -1]], colors='k', linestyles='--')
plt.xscale('log')
plt.xlabel(complexity_label)
plt.ylabel(r'$R^2$')
_ = plt.title(r'Best $R^2$: {:.2} for $\alpha$ = {:.1e}'.format(
    r2_best, complexity_best_ridge))
_ = plt.xlim(complexity_rng[[0, -1]])

Ridge regression with KFold on the training data for various alpha values

This curve shows us the best value for alpha on the training set.

Then we choose to represent the distribution of the model coefficients in two settings :

  • for the OLS regression (without regularization)
  • for the ridge regression (with the optimized alpha)

This is to make sure that the ridge regression really has an impact on the coefficient of the model (and thus to verify that regularisation has a point here)

In [17]:
figsize = np.array(plt.rcParams['figure.figsize']) * np.array([2, 1.2])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=figsize)
fig.tight_layout(pad=5.0)

# Ridge coefficients with the best alpha
ax[0].hist(coefs_best, density=True)
ax[0].set_xlabel(r'Ridge coefficients')
ax[0].set_ylabel('Probability density function')

# OLS coefficients
ax[1].hist(coefs[0], density=True)

Finally, we observe wether this regularisation process has an effect on the model performance in termes of R² score.

While the test R² score is : 0.84

As we are not satisfied by our test R² score regarding the train R² score and the previous test R² score that was higher, we choose to try a more severe regularisation technique in termes of impact on the model coefficients : the Lasso regression.

  1. A second regularisation technique : Lasso regression

As we did with the ridge regression, we first choose to optimize the lasso regression hyperparameter with a cross validation on the train set. And we also represent the coefficient distribution for the OLS regression and the Lasso regression.

In [19]:

We can see with the figure above that the Lasso regularisation has a great impact on the coefficient of the model, it reduces most of the coefficients to zero, conforting us in the idea that the high correlation between features is pushing the model towards creating huge competing coefficients and that a strong regularisation could change that.

We can now see if it had a further impact on the test R² compared to the ridge regularisation.

In [20]:
reg = reg_class(alpha=complexity_best_lasso, **kwargs_lasso)

reg.fit(X_train_pv, y_train_pv)

r2_train = reg.score(X_train_pv, y_train_pv)
r2_test = reg.score(X_test_pv, y_test_pv)

print('While the test R² score is : {:.2f}'.format(r2_test))

The train R² score is : 0.94
While the test R² score is : 0.86

Lasso does better that Ridge, however it does not improve the test R² compared to the OLS and it thus means that eventhough the correlation between features is very high (as the lasso model managed to achieve a comparable R² score with many coefficient turned down to zero), the noise enhanced by the model huge coefficient is not the main issue with our regression.

Our next hypothesis to explain why the model is not performing well on the year 2019 (test set), is that the dataset distribution is not iid, and that there is a shift of distribution across time and especially during the year 2019 (which could have been a very warm year for example).

  1. Study of the data distribution

To test this hypothesis we choose to change our test/train split methode. We randomly select 80% of months for the train set and 20% of months for the test set. This results in similar empirical distributions for both sets, ie we force training and testing to be similar and prevent a time lag.

If the data distribution is indeed the issue with our regression problem, this randomized split technique should improve the test R², and the train and test R² should be much more similar.

We split the data with this new function :

In [21]:
def random_split(random_state, features_a_garder, pv_or_wind):
    df_ici = df_final.copy()

    df_ici['month'] = df_ici['time'].dt.month
    df_ici['sin_month'] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df_ici['month'] / 12)
    df_ici['cos_month'] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df_ici['month'] / 12)
    
    region_cols = [col for col in df_final.columns if col.startswith('region_')]
    calendar_features = ['sin_month', 'cos_month']
    if pv_or_wind == 'pv':
        vre = 'cap_factor_pv'
    else:
        vre = 'cap_factor_wind'

    final_cols = (['time', vre] + 
                    features_a_garder + 
                    calendar_features + 
                    region_cols)

    df_ici = df_ici[final_cols].copy()

    train_df, test_df, train_months, test_months = split_by_random_months(df_ici, prop=0.8, random_state=random_state)

    label = [vre]
    exclude_cols = ['time', 'region_name'] + label
    features_cols = [c for c in train_df.columns if c not in exclude_cols]
    
    train_df = train_df.dropna(subset=[vre])
    X_train_df = train_df[features_cols]
    y_train_df = train_df[vre]
    
    test_df = test_df.dropna(subset=[vre])
    X_test_df = test_df[features_cols]
    y_test_df = test_df[vre]

    return X_train_df, y_train_df, X_test_df, y_test_df


# With the following function allowing us to randomly select months from the dataset 
# to perform a test/train split with the most random distribution possible.

def split_by_random_months(df, prop=0.8, random_state=42):
    df = df.copy()
    df["year_month"] = df["time"].dt.to_period("M")

    months = df["year_month"].unique()

    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_state)
    rng.shuffle(months)

    n_months_train = int(len(months) * prop)
    train_months = months[:n_months_train]
    test_months = months[n_months_train:]

    train_df = df[df["year_month"].isin(train_months)].drop(columns="year_month")
    test_df  = df[df["year_month"].isin(test_months)].drop(columns="year_month")

    return train_df, test_df, train_months, test_months

And we train our OLS model with this new random split

  1. Training of a new supervised regression

We make the hypothesis that a linear regression is a model too simple to capture the link between athmospheric conditions and wind power capacity factor (this hypothesis is motivated by the fact that wind power is proportional to the cube of wind speed).

To verify this we represent the learning curve of an OLS regression with the wind data set (with a randomization of the data set).

In [26]:

test_df_num_norm = (test_df_num - train_df_num.mean()) / train_df_num.std()

train_df_num_norm[features_a_garder] = train_df_num_norm[features_a_garder].replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).fillna(0)
test_df_num_norm[features_a_garder] = test_df_num_norm[features_a_garder].replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).fillna(0)

X_train_wind[features_a_garder] = train_df_num_norm[features_a_garder]
X_test_wind[features_a_garder] = test_df_num_norm[features_a_garder]




# RF Learning Curve

train_sizes = np.linspace(0.05, 1.0, 10)
train_scores = []
test_scores = []

n_train = X_train_wind.shape[0]

for frac in train_sizes:
    n = int(frac * n_train)
    X_sub = X_train_wind.iloc[:n]
    y_sub = y_train_wind.iloc[:n]
    
    model = rf
    model.fit(X_sub, y_sub)
    
    # Score on the training subset
    y_pred_train = model.predict(X_sub)
    train_scores.append(r2_score(y_sub, y_pred_train))
    
    # Score on the full test set
    y_pred_test = model.predict(X_test_wind)
    test_scores.append(r2_score(y_test_wind, y_pred_test))

plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
plt.plot(train_sizes * n_train, train_scores, label="Training score")
plt.plot(train_sizes * n_train, test_scores, label="Test score")
plt.xlabel("Training set size")
plt.ylabel("Score R²")
plt.title("Learning curve Random Forest (chronological split - wind)")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

E.g., non-numpy array/tensor objects with view semantics may contain duplicates after shuffling.
  rng.shuffle(months)

Beyond the data distribution problem (visible when comparing the test R² on the learning curbe and on the previous code cell), this learning curve shows us that the model is overfitting. Thus to improve our R² we decied to try to optimise the model hyperparameters to reduce the model's variance.

  1. Hyperparameter optimization

To optimize the RF model we use OOB-based validation curves : we choose to vary different hyperparameters and to represent the evolution of the OOB error for each variation, this way we can determine the hyperparameter value that minimizes the error, and maximizes the model performance.

We start with the default hyperparameters and we start by optimizing the hyperparameter "n_estimators" which is the number of trees in the forest, it is arguably the most important hyperparameter for forests.

In [31]:
# Optimization of the number of trees (n_estimators)

X_train_wind, y_train_wind, X_test_wind, y_test_wind = dataset_creation(2019, 2019, features_a_garder, 'wind')

# Normalization not necessary for Random Forest
# Values to test for n_estimators
estimator_range = [10, 25, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 500]
oob_errors = []

for n_estimators in estimator_range:
    rf = RandomForestRegressor(
        n_estimators=n_estimators,
        random_state=42,
        oob_score=True,
        n_jobs=-1)
    rf.fit(X_train_wind, y_train_wind)
    oob_error = 1 - rf.oob_score_
    oob_errors.append(oob_error)
    print(f"n_estimators: {n_estimators}, OOB Error: {oob_error:.4f}")

# visualisation
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(estimator_range, oob_errors, marker='o', linestyle='-')
plt.title("Evolution of OOB error as a function of the number of estimators")
plt.xlabel("Number of estimators (n_estimators)")
plt.ylabel("OOB Error (1 - R² OOB)")
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

  1. Training of another new supervised regression

The Random Forest did not performe better than the linear regression, but the manual optimization we did, was not optimal since we optimized parameters by hand and most of all sequenciently.

Knowing this, we want to try another powerful model : XGBoost ; but we want to optimize it with a library made for optimization to try to improve the wind capacity factor estimation as much as possible. We will thus use the library Optuna to optimize our model.

In [35]:
from xgboost import XGBRegressor
In [36]:
import optuna
In [37]:
X_train_wind, y_train_wind, X_test_wind, y_test_wind = dataset_creation(2019, 2019, features_a_garder, 'wind')


# Optuna objectives
def objective(trial):
    params = {
        "n_estimators": trial.suggest_int("n_estimators", 300, 2000),
        "learning_rate": trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 1e-3, 0.2, log=True),
        "max_depth": trial.suggest_int("max_depth", 2, 12),
        "min_child_weight": trial.suggest_float("min_child_weight", 1e-2, 50.0, log=True),
        "subsample": trial.suggest_float("subsample", 0.5, 1.0),
        "colsample_bytree": trial.suggest_float("colsample_bytree", 0.5, 1.0),
        "gamma": trial.suggest_float("gamma", 0.0, 10.0),
        "reg_alpha": trial.suggest_float("reg_alpha", 1e-8, 10.0, log=True),
        "reg_lambda": trial.suggest_float("reg_lambda", 1e-8, 100.0, log=True),
        "objective": "reg:squarederror",
        "random_state": 42,
        "n_jobs": -1,
        "tree_method": "hist", 
    }

    model = XGBRegressor(**params)

    model.fit(
        X_train_wind, y_train_wind,
        eval_set=[(X_test_wind, y_test_wind)],
        verbose=False
    )

    y_pred = model.predict(X_test_wind)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test_wind, y_pred))
    return rmse 

# Here start the optimization, WARNING n_trials is a very important paramater to choose
study = optuna.create_study(direction="minimize")
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=50, show_progress_bar=True)

print("Best hyperparameters:", study.best_params)
print("Best RMSE (val):", study.best_value)

  1. Evaluation of the optimized model
In [38]:
# Training with the best hyperparameters
best_params = study.best_params.copy()
best_params.update({
    "objective": "reg:squarederror",
    "random_state": 42,
    "n_jobs": -1,
    "tree_method": "hist",
})

best_model = XGBRegressor(**best_params)
best_model.fit(X_train_wind, y_train_wind)

y_pred = best_model.predict(X_test_wind)

train_score = best_model.score(X_train_wind, y_train_wind)
mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test_wind, y_pred)
rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test_wind, y_pred))
r2 = r2_score(y_test_wind, y_pred)

print(f"Train R²   : {train_score:.4f}")
print(f"Test R²   : {r2:.4f}")
print(f"MAE  : {mae:.4f}")
print(f"RMSE : {rmse:.4f}")

scatter_plot(y_test_wind, y_pred, "Wind")
#series_time_plot(y_test_wind, y_pred, test_wind, "Wind", region_etude)

Train R²   : 0.9027
Test R²   : 0.6787
MAE  : 0.0360
RMSE : 0.0477
Visualization : Wind

Despite using a library specifically designed for optimization, the model still exhibits signs of overfitting. This suggests that both models may be overly complex relatively to the size of the available dataset.

An interesting approch to capture some of the non-linearity of the wind power production could have been to add new features created from the climate features we had in the data set, like for example the cube of wind speed.
